entries.title: Nepal flood: Death toll tops 1,000 as rescue continues
entries.summary: Nepalese authorities say 4,000 people remain unaccounted for as rescue teams with search dogs comb through mud, rocks and debris.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

Nepalese authorities say 4,000 people remain unaccounted for as rescue teams with search dogs comb through mud, rocks and debris.

The death toll after a massive flash flood last week at the Himalayan border between Nepal and China has risen more than 1,000 people, local authorities said on Tuesday.

In Nepal, 987 deaths have already been reported, with almost 4,000 people still being unaccounted for. In China,16 deaths and 546 missing people have been reported. 

The list of missing people includes some 800 foreign nationals.

Search and rescue teams are still carrying out operations despite difficult conditions and unstable terrain.

Search dogs are also taking part in the search efforts through mud, rocks and debris the flash floods left behind.

Roads were destroyed in places, cutting off access.

Efforts are also being made to locate the some 500 workers believed to be trapped inside the tunnels of twelve hydropower project tunnels, according to Nepalese authorities.

Climate change raises risk for region, PM says

The flash floods on August 28, started as a glacial collapse in the Himalayas triggered a powerful stream of rock, ice and meltwater into the valleys below.

The stream was so powerful that a seismic event of 5.2 magnitude was recorded.

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah reacted to the disaster by emphasizing the need to fight climate change.

"This incident has indicated that the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing with climate change," he posted on social media.

"Therefore, this region must be alert, and at the same time, it is time for us to strongly raise the issue of disasters caused by climate change before the international community."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans
entries.summary: Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.
entries.content:
United States of America

US irks Germany, Europe with Russian G20 invite, press bans

September 1, 2026

Russia's finance minister is at the G20 meeting in Asheville but some key US press corps members are not. The mood was already tense amid the lengthy Iran war and Trump's renewed beef with neighbor Canada.

G20 finance ministers and central bank heads gathered in Asheville, North Carolina for two days of talks.

The session is being overshadowed by dissatisfaction over the White House welcoming Russia to the meeting but not some critical reporters, the war with Iran and its economic fallout, and Donald Trump's latest trade dispute with Canada. 

Who is representing Russia at the meeting?

Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov made an unexpected appearance as talks opened late on Monday. He held a bilateral meeting with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

"We like getting along with everybody," Trump told reporters when asked about the first in-person Russian invite since the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. 

The US currently holds the rotating G20 presidency and so is hosting the session.

The US government told several news agencies on condition of anonymity that Bessent used the meeting to tell Siluanov that the US would not give Russia economic relief until it brings its four-and-a-half-year invasion to a close.

How did European delegates respond?

"Receiving the Russian finance minsiter here sends a troubling signal," German Finance Minsiter Lars Klingbeil said. 

He said he and his European colleagues made clear that they would not appear in the traditional "family photo" alongside the Russian media, saying this was a common EU position.

The photo was ultimately taken without Siluanov and away from the media.

Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domanski told the Reuters news agency that he recognized the right of the G20 hosts to invite guests, but that he was unhappy to see Moscow represented.

"We do not trust Russia. They lie constantly and you need to be really, really cautious while discussing with them," he said. "So for me it would be very difficult to have any kind of conversation with Russia."

Which reporters and outlets were excluded?

As leaders gathered in Asheville, three giants of the US media landscape complained of either no or limited access toe the meeting.

The business-focused Bloomberg News said that its team was not allowed access, while the Wall Street Journal and the New York Times both complained that certain journalists who would typically cover such events were refused media credentials.

Following a challenge from the DJV German journalists' union on Monday, Klingbeil was critical on the matter.

"I believe the press has a completely legitimate interest in reporting openly and freely on this G20 summit," he said. "I consider it unacceptable for journalists or entire editorial teams to be excluded."

Intractable Iran war weighing down global economy

Klingbeil had also said in a German political podcast last week that he would bring a simple message to the US regarding what he called Donald Trump's "irresponsible" war in Iran — that it needed to come to an end. 

Host Bessent, however, was trying to drum up support among allies for the US plans for what it calls "Operation Economic Outcast," an intensified sanction regime against Iran reliant in no small part on third parties outside the US who still do business with Tehran.

Iran has withstood decades of extensive US and western sanctions, but Bessent tried to argue when asked by reporters that it could swiftly be made to collapse if its remaining trading partners joined in.

"I think it could be within weeks or months — and the economy doesn't have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses," he said.

Trump's latest Canada meltdown unsettles allies

The other major source of strain at the meeting was last week's sudden deterioration in trade talks between the US and Canada.

This quickly descended into the tit-for-tat imposition of tariffs, and President Trump launching various social media jabs before unilaterally redesignating Lake Ontario as Lake America, at least on the books in the US. 

Canada's Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne sought to stress that even the recent friction did not impact his participation.

"Canada has always been at the table and constructive, ready to discuss," he told reporters, stressing the need to ensure continued economic growth and "bring back some stability in trade."

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Germany news: FM says Algeria can provide gas supplies
entries.summary: The top diplomat called for Germany to further diversify its energy sources given the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on fuel prices. He said Algeria could become an important supplier of gas in the future.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: FM says Algeria can provide gas supplies

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 1, 2026

The top diplomat called for Germany to further diversify its energy sources given the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on fuel prices. He said Algeria could become an important supplier of gas in the future.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Germany's Foreign Minister Wadephul in Algeria for talks on renewable energy and gas
  • Wadephul stressed the need to "diversify" energy sources, describing Algeria as a "reliable partner"
  • The top diplomat also vowed a measured response to an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month
  • IG Metall union chief says Volkswagen is making a "big mistake" by mulling further job cuts and plant closures

Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Tuesday, September 1.

Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here  to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section Germany to officially blame Russia for attempted drone attack: media reports

Germany to officially blame Russia for attempted drone attack: media reports

The German government reportedly believes a Russian intelligence service was behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month.

Various German media reports citing unnamed sources said Berlin would announce the details of its investigation into the incident, including the finding that Moscow was responsible, later on Tuesday.

The government has not commented on the reports, but Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt are scheduled to give a press conference on the matter in the German capital later this afternoon.

Following the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport on August 4, Berlin referred to a "hybrid attack" and said only that "foreign powers" could be involved. Some lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, but the government stopped short of identifying a culprit.

Media outlets also reported on Tuesday that the German government was preparing countermeasures against Moscow as part of its response. According to Spiegel, those measures could include the expulsion of Russian diplomats and the closure of Russia's consulate in Bonn.

Skip next section German union slams Volkswagen CEO over potential plant closures

German union slams Volkswagen CEO over potential plant closures

The head of the IG Metall union has warned Volkswagen's management it is making a "big mistake" by considering further layoffs and possible plant closures.

Volkswagen is already planning to cut 50,000 jobs by 2030, but the management has said more savings are needed, with the future of several factories uncertain.

In comments published in the Augsburger Allgemeine newspaper on Tuesday, union chief Christiane Benner said she would oppose any closure of the carmaker's plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover or Audi's Neckarsulm site at an upcoming supervisory board meeting on the cost-cutting plans.

"It is a big mistake by Volkswagen management to put the plants in Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and Neckarsulm at risk of closure, seek to cut another 50,000 jobs and at the same time announce that the operating margin must rise from 3.8% most recently to 8%-10% by 2030," Benner said.

She added that the company was required to honor commitments made to workers under an agreement reached in 2024.

Around 30,000 jobs depend on the Emden plant in northern Germany, Benner said, while the Zwickau site is particularly important for eastern Germany.

She argued there was "plenty of time to develop prospects for both sites" and said announcements about further potential cost-cutting measures had only created confusion and undermined morale among workers.

Skip next section Germany 'will not be intimidated' by Russia: Wadephul

Germany 'will not be intimidated' by Russia: Wadephul

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Berlin would offer a measured response to last month's discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport. 

The German government has not officially said who it believes was behind the August 4 incident, although there has been widespread speculation that Moscow was responsible. Russia's embassy in Berlin has denied involvement.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said an investigation into the incident was nearing completion and vowed to provide a clear-cut response in coordination with NATO and EU allies.

News outlets Welt and Politico reported on the weekend that the German government was preparing to announce that Russian intelligence was behind the attempted drone attack.

German media have reported on Tuesday that the federal government would issue an announcement later Tuesday.

When asked to comment, Foreign Minister Wadephul said Germany would not overreact and that its response would be "firm."

"Germany must position itself in such a way that anyone who attacks us knows we will respond. And we are now preparing that response carefully," he told journalists at a press conference in Algiers.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said.

When asked whether Berlin should be worried about a potential counter-response from Moscow, Wadephul said: "Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated."

Skip next section German Foreign Minister talks gas, energy supply in Algiers

German Foreign Minister talks gas, energy supply in Algiers

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul says gas from Algeria could help replenish Germany's gas storage facilities in the future.

"Diversification is absolutely the order of the day," the top diplomat told reporters in Algiers on the second day of his trip to North Africa.

Wadephul described Algeria as a "reliable partner" that was already supplying gas to EU countries Italy and Spain.

"Both in terms of securing critical raw materials and in matters of energy security, we need reliable partners and resilient supply chains, particularly in our immediate neighbourhood," the minister said.

Wadephul added that Algeria's potential as a future supplier of green hydrogen would only make the partnership more important.

Energy supply under pressure

Wadephul's visit comes at a time when the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Middle East is heaping pressure on energy supplies.

"It is quite clear that we must diversify. We need multiple sources of supply," Wadephul said.

Additionally, Germany's gas storage facilities are currently only about 50% full, with the government-mandated target of 70% by November seen as impossible to reach. Storage facilities were 67% full at the same time last year. But despite the low levels, the government has said there is no danger of a gas shortage.  

Wadephul met with Algerian Energy Minister Mohamed Arkab on Tuesday, where his focus was "trying to negotiate long-term contracts for Germany."

"If that is possible, then we will have another reliable source here, which is of course also important for our gas storage facilities," Wadephul said.

The foreign minister is traveling with an economic delegation and was also expected to meet representatives from German companies. He was also due to meet with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune.

On Monday, Wadephul was in Tunisia where he met Head of State Kais Saied and his counterpart, Mohammed Ali Nafti.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag! from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

You join us as German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul seeks to secure gas contracts on a visit to Algeria.

The top diplomat stressed that Germany needed to diversify its energy sources at a time when the effective closure of the Middle East's Strait of Hormuz is constraining energy supply and pushing up prices.  

We're also expecting an announcement from Berlin this afternoon outlining a response to the discovery in August of a drone laden with explosives at Leipzig airport.

Meanwhile, the boss of Germany's IG Metall union has criticized the management of automaker Volkswagen for considering more layoffs and potential plant closures.

Stay with us for all these stories and more.

entries.title: Iran says it will return to ceasefire if US does
entries.summary: Speaking on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iran's president Pezeshkian called on the US to return to the terms of an interim ceasefire deal.
entries.content:
Iran

Iran says it will return to ceasefire if US does

September 1, 2026

Speaking on the sidelines of the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, Iran's president Pezeshkian called on the US to return to the terms of an interim ceasefire deal.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Tuesday said Tehran would reciprocate any US move that signals a return to the collapsed interim ceasefire deal.

"I state explicitly that if the United States returns to its commitments under the ... memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately take reciprocal action," Pezeshkian said on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Pezeshkian accused the US of "reneging on its commitments" under the agreement, which fell apart in June, with both sides accusing the other of violating the agreement's terms.

At the time, the US carried out strikes on Iranian targets after what it called "continued aggression" against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, with an Iranian drone striking a Panama-flagged tanker. 

Tehran has repeatedly said it ⁠will ​allow free navigation through the Strait, but on its terms. A diplomatic solution to the conflict remains elusive. 

Pezeshkian's comments come shortly after the US and Iran traded fire for the first time in over a month. The US said it struck Iranian minelaying forces on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday and Iran targeted US forces in the Middle East in response. 

US President Donald Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday that there will be a "response" to the Iranian attacks, but said the latest strikes did not mean a return to full-scale war.

Putin and Xi meet at SCO summit

Pezeshkian is due to have talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin later Tuesday.

The meeting takes place as Russia's full-scale invasion into Ukraine continues to rumble on for more than four years.

Earlier, Putin met Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has provided Russia with implicit economic backing during the Ukraine war.

According to Xi, the China-Russia pact has become "more solid" and that its "prospects will be even brighter."

On his side, Putin said the two countries' cooperation was "successfully developing on all fronts."

The SCO is a bloc promoted by Russia and China as an alternative to Western power, which has in the past mostly served for economic discussions, with Moscow and Beijing pushing its significance in recent years.

Its 10 members also include India and Pakistan, while its 15 "dialogue partners" being Turkey and Qatar, amongst others.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Apple's new CEO John Ternus makes AI top priority
entries.summary: John Ternus is just the third Apple CEO in 30 years. His primary challenge is to correct the company's faltering AI strategy to preserve its position as a big tech leader.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

John Ternus is just the third Apple CEO in 30 years. His primary challenge is to correct the company's faltering AI strategy to preserve its position as a big tech leader.

On September 1, a new era begins at Apple as John Ternus becomes just the third man to hold the CEO role at the tech giant since 1997.

Ternus was announced as Tim Cook's successor back in April, bringing Cook's 15 years at the helm of one of the world's biggest companies to an end. Since then, Ternus, a leading hardware engineer at the company, has been working closely alongside Cook in preparation for the big job.

Just as Cook had when he took over from the iconic Steve Jobs, Ternus has big shoes to fill. Apple's share price has increased by more than 2,000% since Cook took over in 2011 and the company has sold more than 3.1 billion iPhones in that time.

Ternus faces a range of challenges at Apple, but his ability to keep the company at the top will hinge on how he reshapes its AI strategy.

Apple has struggled to successfully embrace the technology so far, with critics saying it has fallen far behind its rivals.

September 9: John Ternus makes public debut

Ternus will make his public debut as CEO at Apple's Autumn product launch event on September 9. Dubbed "Surprise and Shine," Ternus is expected to announce the company's first foldable iPhone as well as a new version of an AI-powered Siri, Apple's virtual assistant.

Francisco Jeronimo, VP for Data and Analytics at tech research group IDC, said Apple's forthcoming announcements were planned during Cook's time in charge and that it will be 2027 before the direction Ternus wants to take the company in becomes apparent.

"Of course, September 9 will be quite an important milestone for the company around foldables and around innovation," he told DW.

"But I don't think we have seen anything that could indicate that Apple is behaving in a different way or is showing a different kind of strategy because Tim Cook is not in the job anymore — yet."

Apple's huge AI challenge

What observers will be looking out for from Ternus on September 9 is the extent to which he focuses his remarks on AI.

While it was already undeniable when he was announced in April that the artificial intelligence boom would be pivotal to his time at the helm, it has become even clearer in the five months since the unveiling that the AI revolution is here to stay.

"It's becoming clear that AI is not a fad, is not something that will go away in the next two or three years," said Jeronimo. "It's something that will dictate the future of most tech companies and indeed all companies."

He reckons AI could be "the most consequential technology" for Apple because it could either help it maintain its lofty position or create a set of daunting challenges.

The biggest challenge he sees is that Apple doesn't "control" AI infrastructure the way it could previously in terms of designing and controlling both the hardware and software for its key products.

"Maybe that will be what John Ternus will be doing differently from Tim Cook, because at the moment, even if Apple built their own AI technology, the reality is that they still depend on someone else," he added.

Apple's reliance on other companies in the AI realm has led it into unfamiliar territory. It struck a deal with OpenAI in 2024 to integrate ChatGPT into the iPhone, but that has led to a bitter dispute between the companies. Apple sued OpenAI earlier this year, alleging that the AI company stole its trade secrets.

Earlier this year, it announced a deal with Google, whereby the search giant's Gemini models would be used for Apple's own AI models and its new AI-powered version of Siri.

"The risk for Apple is to become less relevant in a world where companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are leading in terms of technology, in terms of awareness, in terms of services and potentially in terms of hardware," said Jeronimo.

For decades, Apple's success has been built on its physical products, from the iPad to the iPhone.

"If devices from OpenAI become available, that could be very, very risky for Apple. They could completely disrupt the experience and the way we interact with technology. And if Apple is not on the front of that innovation, that is a big risk," he said.

A combination of Jobs and Cook?

Ternus' background as an engineer who worked on Apple's core products, as well as innovations such as the Apple Watch and AirPods, means he will be expected to lead the way on new AI-driven products for the company.

He also played a central role championing Apple's shift to designing its own chips instead of relying on external suppliers like Intel — precisely the kind of independence Apple would like to achieve when it comes to AI.

Jeronimo thinks Apple still has big advantages, given its massive volume of users as well as the company culture of having dominated innovation in tech for decades. He thinks if Apple can get to grips with AI under Ternus, it could lead to huge success: "What we will see in the next years will dictate whether Apple is on the right track or if they are really struggling." 

For Ternus, the first task will be to simply fit smoothly and convincingly into a role that both Jobs and Cook undeniably made their own. "Steve Jobs was the guru of innovation and disruption and Tim Cook was the guru of execution," saidJeronimo.

"I think John Ternus can be a combination of both."

Edited by: Rob Mudge

entries.title: Times Square stabbing in NYC leaves 1 dead, assailant killed
entries.summary: A woman armed with two kitchen knives killed one person and wounded another in New York City's Times Square before police fatally shot her. Authorities said the attack was random and unprovoked.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

A woman armed with two kitchen knives killed one person and wounded another in New York City's Times Square before police fatally shot her. Authorities said the attack was random and unprovoked.

A woman with two kitchen knives fatally stabbed one person and wounded another in New York City's popular Times Square on Monday before police shot and killed her, officials said.

The knife attack occurred just before 4:30 pm near a police substation outside One Times Square, the building known for hosting the city's annual New Year's Eve ball drop.

What do we know about the Times Square knife attack?

New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the 49-year-old suspect from the borough of Queens pulled the knives from a shopping bag and stabbed a 68-year-old man in the abdomen as he exited a subway station with his wife. She then attacked a 32-year-old woman, stabbing her in the abdomen. Both victims were hospitalized, with the young woman dying of her wounds. The older man is currently in stable condition, police said.

Officers surrounded the suspect and attempted to get her to drop the knives before deploying a Taser, which also failed to stop her, according to Tisch.

The suspect reportedly told officers, "I'm not dropping anything, I would rather kill both of you," before advancing toward them with the knives raised.

Multiple officers then opened fire, with bystander video showing her falling to the ground, where officers handcuffed her and administered first aid. She was later pronounced dead.

What did the authorities say?

"This was an extraordinarily dangerous situation unfolding in the heart of Times Square, the crossroads of the world," Tisch said.

She added the attack was random and unprovoked.

Tisch said the suspect had a documented history of mental health contacts with police, including incidents in 2018 and 2019, but no prior arrests.

Investigators do not believe the attack was terrorism-related, and police have not released the victims' identities pending notification of family.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani, told a news conference, "We know that those families' lives have been shattered by what took place today, and we will continue to hold them close as the hours and days and weeks continue from this moment."

Both Mamdani and Tisch credited the responding officers, saying their actions likely prevented further casualties.

The incident marks the second fatal stabbing in Times Square this year, following a similar attack in May, even as the New York City's overall homicide rate has dropped sharply to one of its lowest totals in decades.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: Ukraine updates: Russia hits Kyiv for sixth straight day
entries.summary: Deadly attacks both in Ukraine and Russia continue as European Union defense ministers discuss the "hybrid" threat from Moscow in Europe. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine updates: Russia hits Kyiv for sixth straight day

Published September 1, 2026last updated September 1, 2026

Deadly attacks both in Ukraine and Russia continue as European Union defense ministers discuss the "hybrid" threat from Moscow in Europe. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Follow this blog for the latest news on Russia's war in Ukraine on September 1, 2026.

  • Russian strikes Kyiv, Odesa on first day of school year, killing at least 12

  • EU ministers focus on Ukraine air defenses, military support at Ireland talks

  • Drones trigger brief NATO response at Estonia's border with Russia

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

EU's Kallas says more interceptors needed to shield Ukrainian cities

On Tuesday, European Union defense ministers discussed Ukraine's shortage of interceptor missiles needed to protect cities and civilians.

"July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine," the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Tuesday about the deadly wave of strikes on Ukraine.

"Russia is really escalating, to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible, to break them," she said on the sidelines of a gathering of EU defense ministers in Wicklow in Ireland.

Against that backdrop, she said securing additional interceptors remains difficult because some countries face security pressures closer to home.

"We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine," Kallas said.

Beyond efforts to bolster air defenses, the EU is also working to unlock additional financial support for Ukraine's armed forces in the coming days.

Skip next section Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany says response to drone find near Ukrainian plane will be measured

Germany's foreign minister said Berlin would respond in a measured way to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. 

Johann Wadephul said the government was coordinating its approach with NATO and European Union partners.

The case sparked widespread speculation that Russia was responsible, though Berlin has not publicly assigned blame.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pledged a clear-cut response.

Despite declining to publicly assign responsibility, Wadephul stressed Germany would not be deterred by the incident.

"Germany will not be intimidated in any way, and that will continue to be the fundamental stance of our policy," Wadephul said, adding that Berlin "stands side by side with our Ukrainian partner."

"Russia must know that Germany is a stabilizing force in Europe, one that is always prepared to negotiate, but which will not be intimidated in any way."

Skip next section Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine says Russian missile and drone assault hits Kyiv, Odesa

Ukraine's air force said Russia struck at least 28 locations in overnight attacks that continued into Tuesday, with debris falling at several additional sites.

The attack targeted Kyiv and the Odesa region and involved ballistic, cruise and anti-radar missiles, along with more than 200 drones and decoys.

At least 11 people were killed in the capital region:

  • Seven people were killed in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district; three others were wounded, including a child.
  • One Indian citizen was reported among those killed
  • One person was killed in the Holosiivskyi district after a building was hit and caught fire.
  • Three people were killed and 12 were injured elsewhere in the Kyiv region.

In Odesa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian strike "deliberately damaged a border crossing point on the border with Romania, as well as export infrastructure."

Skip next section Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Ukraine reports August strikes on 54 Russian 'Shadow Fleet' ships

Russia and Ukraine are not only battling for dominance in the air with drones, but are also increasingly taking the drone war to the seas.

The commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert Brov, said Tuesday that his force struck 54 Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in August.

He did not immediately provide additional details.

Separately, Russia's state news agency Tass reported that Russia attacked "more than 150 seagoing vessels involved in military cargo deliveries for the Ukrainian army, as well as accompanying patrol boats, during the summer."

At least 70 of those attacks were recorded in August.

Skip next section EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

EU defense ministers meet in Ireland to discuss Ukraine air defenses

European Union defense ministers are gathering in Wicklow, south of Dublin, for talks that are expected to focus on bolstering Ukraine's air defenses.

Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes.

There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe.

The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv.

The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion.

The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries.

Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy.

EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine.

Skip next section NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO jets scrambled after drones briefly enter Estonian airspace

NATO military aircraft were scrambled overnight after drones flew close to Estonia's border and briefly entered Estonian airspace, the country's Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said.

The aircraft were launched from Amari Air Base, Tsahkna wrote in a post on social media.

"NATO reacted swiftly and exactly as planned. The Alliance is vigilant and ready to protect Allied territory," he added.

It was not immediately clear who launched the drones.

The incident highlights ongoing security concerns along NATO's eastern flank and is seen as a consequence of Russia's continuing war against Ukraine.

Skip next section Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russian strike on Kyiv railway depot kills 7

Russia targeted Ukraine's capital for a sixth day in a row, including a ballistic missile strike on a railway depot in Kyiv that killed seven people.

"The ballistic strike took the lives of 7 people, 6 of whom were our employees. 1 colleague is in hospital with injuries," Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, chief executive of Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine's state-owned railway network said, adding that "there is extensive destruction."

Emergency services said eight people were killed and five wounded in Kyiv, including three children, as fires broke out across several parts of the capital during the overnight attacks.

Elsewhere in the Kyiv region, one person was killed and nine others, including a child, were injured after missiles and drones struck an apartment building and a business facility in Boryspil.

The attacks marked the sixth consecutive day of Russian strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region.

Russia's Defense Ministry said it targeted military and energy facilities in Kyiv, Odesa, and nearby areas.

Across the border in Russia's Belgorod region, one person was killed in a Ukrainian attack, acting Governor Alexander Shuvayev said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

European defense ministers are meeting in Ireland today and are expected to hear from Ukraine's new acting defense minister, Yevgeniy Khmara.

He is likely to point to the latest wave of Russian attacks, now entering a sixth straight day, as Moscow continues its campaign against Kyiv and surrounding areas.

Ukrainian officials have repeatedly argued that the sustained bombardment underscores the urgent need for additional air defense systems.

The meeting comes as several European countries are also strengthening their own military capabilities, partly in response to a growing number of drone-related incidents near their borders.

Overnight, Estonia reported a new drone incursion into its airspace, adding to concerns about regional security.

We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

entries.title: AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond
entries.summary: The AfD's lead candidate in the upcoming election aims to turn his small federal state into a blueprint for right-wing extremist politics across Germany.
entries.content:
Germany

AfD's Ulrich Siegmund has plans for Saxony-Anhalt and beyond

September 1, 2026

The AfD's lead candidate in the upcoming election aims to turn his small federal state into a blueprint for right-wing extremist politics across Germany.

All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of a state election on Sunday that could trigger a political earthquake across Germany.

Though the state is small, with a population of just 2 million — and with economic strength and life expectancy the lowest of any of Germany's 16 federal states — a victory for the Alternative for Germany (AfD) could usher in the first far-right government in the history of post-World-War-II Germany.

The AfD's lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, and polls show him well in the lead. The only open question seems to be whether the AfD will be able to secure an absolute majority of the seats in Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which would allow it to govern alone. This would appear to be Siegmund's only path to the state premiership, as the other parties have said they will not enter a coalition with the AfD.

Things are going well for the 35-year-old Siegmund. As he tours his state on the campaign trail, he draws crowds — even in small towns. He's often surrounded by a swarm of international journalists: from Canadian and Danish television, Swiss broadcasting, the BBC and the British magazine The Economist, alongside dozens of reporters from across Germany. Everyone wants to know: Who is Ulrich Siegmund?

The candidate was born in the small town of Havelberg, Saxony-Anhalt, in 1990. He joined the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at age 19, only to leave the party five years later and join the AfD. A former perfume salesman, he cuts a dynamic and athletic figure: slim, handsome and fresh-faced.

Above all, he is cheerful — playing the role of a charismatic charmer in his public appearances. When he steps into town squares to a cheering crowd, he beams back, shaking hands and cracking jokes. Nothing about him seems forced; he visibly enjoys the campaign grind.

"I don't know when there was last such a high approval rating, even among young people," Siegmund told DW. "It's simply enormous." He speaks quickly, articulately and with practiced ease.

AfD campaign pushes policies with 'high-gloss marketing'

Even critical observers in Saxony-Anhalt can't help but admit that the AfD has all the momentum in this election.

"The AfD's campaign events run like clockwork, both logistically and in terms of political strategy," observed David Begrich of Miteinander, an organization based in the state capital of Magdeburg that fights right-wing extremism. "It is high-gloss marketing of their own policies."

But what exactly do the AfD's policies aim to achieve? To judge by Siegmund's campaign speeches, the goal is a return to a bygone era — a time before Germany viewed itself as a country of immigration, when electricity came from nuclear power plants rather than wind turbines, and when LGBTQ+ rights were not yet recognized. Siegmund wants to pursue, as he says in his campaign speeches, politics "from the people, for the people!"

Apparently, that doesn't include all the people living in the state. The AfD's "100-day immediate action plan" contains some radical policies, including a key promise to "deport from minute one" foreign nationals who have no legal right to stay, but whose presence is tolerated for humanitarian reasons, many of whom have found work and established their lives in Germany.

The action plan also calls for funding cuts to pro-democracy NGOs, forcing refugees to work and prioritizing a love for the German homeland over social diversity. There are significant legal doubts, however, about whether a state government actually has the authority to implement all these pledges.

Controversial figures behind the scenes

There are also doubts over the "clean" image that Siegmund has cultivated. He has not been able to escape the allegations of cronyism that have dogged the AfD, after it was reported that several of the party's state and federal lawmakers secured well-paid jobs for their friends and relatives in the offices of other AfD officials.

Siegmund himself found a position for his own father. While not illegal, the move was poorly received, even within his own party.

Then there are the people behind Siegmund, those who support him as leader of the AfD's parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt. According to the daily newspaper Die Welt, the group employs four former members of a now-banned neo-Nazi organization, the Heimattreue Deutsche Jugend (German Youth Loyal to the Homeland). Before it was outlawed, the group openly admired Adolf Hitler's Nazism and adhered to his racial ideology, one that led to the murder of 6 million Jews and hundreds of thousands of Sinti and Roma in the Holocaust.

Siegmund himself appears to have no qualms about associating with supporters who have tattoos or clothes with neo-Nazi symbols. DW observed him appearing arm-in-arm with men wearing neo-Nazi attire and sporting tattoos such as the Black Sun, a recognized symbol among neo-Nazis.

AfD wants to 'turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground'

But what would all this mean if the AfD actually did take power after the September 6 election?

"There are clear indications that if the AfD were to enter government, it would turn Saxony-Anhalt into a testing ground for the whole country," said Begrich. "Just how far can one go in overriding the written — and perhaps even more importantly, the unwritten — rules of democratic culture in a federal state?"

For that reason, many churches, trade unions, civil society organizations and political parties have warned against an AfD victory. Begrich shares their concerns.

"Naturally, things will become difficult, above all, for those in society who either belong to minorities or do not fit into the AfD's ideological worldview," he said. "The social climate would inevitably shift to an authoritarian regimentation — and that poses a problem for people who need liberal openness in society as they need air to breathe."

Like many critics, Begrich believes that winning Saxony-Anhalt is only the first step for a party that wants to take over the entire country.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Duane 'Keffe D' Davis guilty
entries.summary: The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years. Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.
entries.content:
September 1, 2026

The jury reached a verdict in less than three hours in a case that had been unsolved for nearly 30 years. Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

A Las Vegas jury on Monday found former gang leader, Duane "Keffe D" Davis, guilty of orchestrating the killing of hip hop artist Tupac Shakur, following nine days of testimony.

Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.

Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.

Verdict reached in under three hours

It took jurors less than three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that has, up until now, been unsolved for almost three decades.

Sixty three-year-old Davis was convicted of murder with the use of a deadly weapon and could be sentenced to life in prison.

Davis, a one-time leader of the South Side Compton Crips gang, is the only person ever to have been charged in Shakur’s murder.

In closing arguments, Clark County Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal told jurors that Davis acquired a gun and “went hunting” for Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion “Suge” Knight after they beat up Davis’ nephew earlier that night.

Palal said that Davis’ accounts of the killing evolved over the years but maintained that those differences showed Davis’ changing motivations and efforts to protect himself.

Palal argued that a key detail remained consistent throughout and that was that Davis repeatedly placed himself inside the white Cadillac from which the shots were fired.

Davis, the sole surviving suspect

Davis is the only person still alive among the four men prosecutors say were in the Cadillac from which shots were fired. The man who prosecutors say originally gave the gun to Davis is also dead.

Police ​had long suspected Davis of involvement in Shakur's murder but could not charge him due to a lack of concrete evidence.

That was until Davis went public with his version of events in media appearances and a memoir, which along with recordings of his secret meetings with investigators, made up the bulk of the prosecution’s ​case.

Davis told the judge that he planned to appeal the verdict. He had pleaded not guilty to the single count of murder using a deadly weapon.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: US Supreme Court allows Trump ballroom project to proceed
entries.summary: The ruling was backed by five of the court's six conservative justices. US President Donald Trump praised the decision in a post on his Truth Social platform.
entries.content:
United States of America

US Supreme Court allows Trump ballroom project to proceed

August 31, 2026

The ruling was backed by five of the court's six conservative justices. US President Donald Trump praised the decision in a post on his Truth Social platform.

The US Supreme Court on Monday allowed US President Donald Trump's administration to continue with the $400 million (€345 million) White House ballroom construction project for now.

The ruling was backed by five ‌of the court's six conservative justices who said that the plaintiffs in the case likely didn't have the legal right to challenge the case.

Court votes 5-4 to lift lower court's order

"This Court has not found standing in circumstances like these before. To the contrary, we have repeatedly held that mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify as a concrete and particularized injury," under the US Constitution, the five justices wrote in their ruling.

"Perhaps nearly any government action or project offends someone's sensibilities," they added.

Chief Justice John Roberts joined the court's three liberal-leaning justices in dissenting from the latest order, calling the construction “likely unlawful" because it hasn't been approved by Congress.

"Today’s decision is no victory for the separation of powers," Roberts wrote.

Trump welcomes Supreme Court ruling

"I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favor of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C." Trump said.

National Trust for Historic Preservation vs. Trump

The nonprofit National Trust for Historic Preservation first brought the matter after the East Wing was torn down and work began on a 90,000-square-foot (8,360-square-meter) ballroom in the the biggest structural change to the White House in over 70 years.

The Trump administration had asked the nation's highest court to intervene after federal courts determined that the project needed to be halted on the grounds of it not having congressional approval.

US Justice Department lawyers previously justified the need for a secure ballroom, pointing to the July 8 missile threat against Air Force One when Trump was flown out of Turkey aboard a secret flight and other recent assassination attempts.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
